title: The soup kitchen
hook: Ottoman imarets fed the poor daily

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hammam, the bathhouse near the mosque, where a town got clean side by side. Your line was: clean together. What refreshing thing did you share, and with whom? Day one thousand seventeen.

A row of great copper pots, already bubbling before the sun is fully up. A cook stirs with a ladle as long as an arm. Outside the door a line is forming: a student with a bowl, an old widow, a traveler still dusty from the road, a man who has not eaten since yesterday. Nobody at the door asks for a coin. Nobody asks for a name. The bowls go out full, and the cooks start the next pot. This is not a story about one kind neighbor. It's about a building that was made to do this every day, whether anyone felt generous that morning or not. In the Ottoman lands it had a name. Today: the soup kitchen.
screen: `COPPER POTS BEFORE SUNRISE.` → `A LINE AT THE DOOR.` → `NOBODY ASKS FOR A COIN.`

segments.voice: The Ottomans called it an imaret. Often it stood beside a mosque, inside a larger complex that might also hold a school, a guest house, sometimes a hospital. And the food came from the idea we met a few days ago, the waqf, the endowment. Someone with means gave land or shops or rents forever, and the income paid for bread and soup, cooks and firewood, long after the giver was gone. So the meal at the door did not depend on anyone's mood. It was written into the deed. Who ate? The deeds that survive set out the order, and it varied from place to place: students and teachers, travelers, the poor of the neighborhood, the staff themselves. Historians read these deeds closely, because they show charity planned like a kitchen schedule. Why build such a thing? The Qur'an describes the righteous this way, in Pickthall's words: "And feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him, (Saying): We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you." Look at that last line. No reward. Not even thanks. The bowl is not a trade. And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari to have told people to feed the hungry, visit the sick, and set captives free. One plain instruction in a short list. The imaret took that line and gave it a roof, a chimney, and a budget. A kitchen that keeps cooking is a promise kept in public. Soup for all.
screen: `THE IMARET STOOD BESIDE THE MOSQUE.` · `PAID FOR BY AN ENDOWMENT, FOREVER.` · `NO REWARD, NOT EVEN THANKS.` · `FEED THE HUNGRY: A PLAIN INSTRUCTION.` · then, large: `WE FEED YOU, FOR THE SAKE OF ALLAH ONLY.`

segments.voice: The practice: feed someone, and plan it now. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who could use a meal. A neighbor who has been ill. A friend with a new baby. A coworker who skips lunch. Or a stranger you'll never meet, through a food bank near you. Picture the bowl, the plate, the bag of groceries. Choose what you'll give and when. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer as you plan. If not, just keep their face in mind and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Imaret. The Ottoman kitchen beside the mosque, paid for by an endowment so the bowls went out every day. Today's word.
Your line: soup for all. Today, feed someone, a meal, a snack, a donation, and ask for nothing back, not even thanks. Day one thousand seventeen.

howItsDone: Mosques and Muslim charities often run community kitchens and food drives, especially in Ramadan, when meals to break the fast are often shared freely with anyone who comes.

notes: Editor pass: hook no longer opens on steam (day 1016's hook did); review line reworded to match 1016's actual carry; dropped the unsourced 'all built around one place of prayer'; 'original' changed from an etymology of imaret (claims rule) to طعام, food, the word in 76:8.
Claims rule: the outline says imarets fed the poor 'daily'; the script says the bowls went out every day and that the order of eaters varied by deed. Confirm with a historian of Ottoman imarets.
Hadith number: 'feed the hungry, visit the sick, free the captive' is given as Sahih al-Bukhari 5373; it also appears elsewhere in Bukhari (e.g. 5649). Confirm the number.
Pickthall 76:8–9 quoted from memory, matching wording used elsewhere in this path; confirm.
The reference to 'the waqf, a few days ago' points back to day 1013.
